To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the combination of two drugs (amikacin and vanomycin) was more effective against S. aureus than each drug alone when the bacteria were exposed to a fluctuating concentration of antibiotics representative of clinical situations; (ii) the static TKS performed with constant drug concentrations over 1 day did not allow to identify any advantage of the combination.

in vitro static and in vitro dynamic assays can be used to evaluate the potential benefit of antibiotic combinations, but that dynamic assays are better suited for evaluating the efficacy of antibiotic combinations in situations of high bacterial load, as in severe infections.

(1) in vitro static and time-kill assays are both relevant tools to study the activity of antibiotic combinations, (2) the static assays are easier to implement and are useful to evaluate the effect of a combination on small inocula, (3) dynamic assays are more demanding but are useful to evaluate a combination on large inocula and over a longer duration.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new in vitro dynamic assay to assess the efficacy of an antibiotic combination on large bacterial inocula.
the evaluation of in vitro static versus dynamic assays to assess the efficacy of an antibiotic combination against two different inocula of S. aureus.
the development of a new in vitro dynamic model to predict the efficacy of an antibiotic combination in severe infections.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the static assay was not able to identify the benefit of the combination whereas the dynamic assay identified the benefit of the drug combination on the large inoculum.
the static assay performed with a small bacterial inoculum was unable to identify the benefit of the antibiotic combination, while the dynamic assay performed with a large bacterial inoculum did.
static and dynamic assays can be complementary to assess combination effects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

static TKS performed over less than 48 hours are poorly representative of the clinical situation and that dynamic TKS should be implemented to assess the efficacy of antibiotic combinations against large bacterial inocula.

, for the treatment of severe bacterial infections, the in vitro evaluation of the efficacy of antibiotic combinations should be performed using dynamic assays over the whole expected treatment period.
the use of static assays is insufficient to evaluate the efficacy against large inocula of an antibiotic combination in severe infections.
The main takeaway from our work is that
static assays should not be the only tool to predict the efficacy of an antibiotic combination.
the in vitro evaluation of the activity of an antibiotic combination should not be restricted to static assays.
in vitro dynamic assays are more relevant than static assays to evaluate the benefits of antibiotic combinations in the context of severe bacterial infections.
